section: 15.8 Exactness and approximation in an element calculation
text:
15.8 Exactness and approximation in an element calculation
The rule
\[
  p\leq2n_g-1
\]
applies to the complete scalar integrand expressed in the reference coordinate \(\xi\). For the present two-node bar, the affine mapping makes \(J\) constant and \(\mathbf{B}\) constant, so the degrees are easy to identify.
If material properties or loading are non-polynomial functions of \(\xi\), no finite-degree exactness guarantee follows. The quadrature result is then generally approximate. Increasing the number of Gauss–Legendre points and examining the change in the element matrix, element vector, or final finite element response provides a practical convergence check.
The degree counts in the table rely on the affine mapping of the two-node bar, for which both \(J\) and its inverse are constant. In more general element mappings, these quantities may vary with position and must also be included when determining the degree of the complete integrand. Those cases will be considered when the corresponding element formulations are introduced.

title: 15  Gauss–Legendre quadrature for the two-node bar
text:
15.9 The element-level mathematical procedure
After the exact transformation to the reference coordinate, the element stiffness matrix and consistent distributed-load vector have the forms
\[
  \mathbf{K}_e
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  E\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  A\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)
  J\,d\xi
\]
and
\[
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  q(\xi)
  J\,d\xi.
\]
For the present affine two-node bar, \(J=L_e/2\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are constant. They remain visible in the complete transformed integrands because they contribute to the element quantities and must be accounted for when selecting the quadrature rule.
The quadrature order is determined from the complete scalar entries of these transformed integrands. If their highest polynomial degrees are \(d_K\) and \(d_q\), respectively, the minimum numbers of Gauss–Legendre points required for exact integration are
\[
  n_K
  =
  \left\lceil\frac{d_K+1}{2}\right\rceil,
  \qquad
  n_q
  =
  \left\lceil\frac{d_q+1}{2}\right\rceil,
\]
because an \(n_g\)-point Gauss–Legendre rule is exact for polynomials of degree up to \(2n_g-1\). If the stiffness matrix and load vector are accumulated using the same quadrature rule, the number of points must satisfy
\[
  n_g
  =
  \max(n_K,n_q).
\]
For a selected rule with quadrature points \(\xi_g\) and weights \(w_g\), define
\[
  x_g=x(\xi_g),
  \qquad
  \mathbf{N}_g=\mathbf{N}(\xi_g),
  \qquad
  \mathbf{B}_g=\mathbf{B}(\xi_g),
\]
together with
\[
  E_g=E(x_g),
  \qquad
  A_g=A(x_g),
  \qquad
  q_g=q(x_g)=q(\xi_g).
\]
The element quantities are then evaluated as
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf{K}_e
  \approx
  \sum_{g=1}^{n_g}
  w_g
  \mathbf{B}_g^{\mathsf T}
  E_gA_g
  \mathbf{B}_g
  J
  }
\]
and
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  \approx
  \sum_{g=1}^{n_g}
  w_g
  \mathbf{N}_g^{\mathsf T}
  q_g
  J.
  }
\]
Each approximation becomes an equality when the selected rule integrates every scalar entry of the corresponding transformed integrand exactly. Once \(\mathbf{K}_e\) and \(\mathbf{f}_e^q\) have been evaluated, they are assembled using the local-to-global operations established in the preceding MiniFEM chapters.

title: 15  Gauss–Legendre quadrature for the two-node bar
text:
15.10 Verification against the closed-form element
The closed-form element results derived earlier provide reference values for the quadrature calculations. For constant \(EA\), the exact stiffness matrix is
\[
  \mathbf{K}_e
  =
  \frac{EA}{L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & -1\\
  -1 & 1
  \end{bmatrix},
\]
while, for a uniform distributed load \(q\), the exact consistent load vector is
\[
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  =
  \frac{qL_e}{2}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
One-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature reproduces both closed-form results exactly. This agreement checks the combined use of the coordinate mapping, Jacobian, transformed integrands, quadrature point, weight, and accumulation. Its validity is limited to these particular integrands, whose degrees do not exceed one.
The linearly varying load provides the complementary check. Its quadratic load-vector integrands are not integrated exactly by the one-point rule, even though that rule recovers their correct aggregate force. The two-point rule reproduces the closed-form consistent load vector and therefore recovers both the total force and its correct nodal distribution.






TipExercises




Expand every entry of \(\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}EA\mathbf{B}J\) for constant \(EA\) and verify its polynomial degree in \(\xi\).
Evaluate the constant-\(EA\) stiffness matrix using the two-point rule and verify explicitly that it agrees with the one-point and closed-form results.
For a uniform distributed load, evaluate both scalar entries of the consistent load vector separately using one-point quadrature.
Let \(q_1=0\) and \(q_2=q_0\). Compare the one- and two-point load vectors and verify that both have the correct total force while only the two-point vector is consistent with exact integration.
Suppose \(EA\) varies linearly with \(\xi\). Determine the minimum Gauss–Legendre rule required for exact stiffness integration for the present affine two-node element.
Suppose \(EA\) is constant and \(q(\xi)\) is quadratic. Determine the degree of each consistent load-vector integrand and the minimum exact Gauss–Legendre rule.









ImportantKey points to remember




Rewriting an element integral from \(x\) to \(\xi\), transforming \(dx=J\,d\xi\), transforming derivatives, and mapping \(\xi_g\) to \(x_g\) are exact operations. Numerical approximation begins only when the transformed integral is replaced by a finite Gauss–Legendre sum.
The quadrature weight \(w_g\) belongs to the numerical integration rule, whereas the Jacobian \(J\) belongs to the coordinate transformation. Their product \(w_gJ\) combines two factors with different origins.
Matrix and vector quadrature is ordinary scalar quadrature applied entry by entry. At each Gauss–Legendre point, the complete matrix or vector integrand is formed and its weighted contribution is accumulated.
The quadrature order must be selected from the degree of the complete transformed scalar integrand. A rule with \(n_g\) points integrates every polynomial of degree \(p\leq2n_g-1\) exactly.
For a straight two-node bar with constant \(EA\), the stiffness integrands have degree zero, so one-point quadrature is exact.
For a uniform distributed load, the consistent load-vector integrands have degree one, so one-point quadrature is exact. For a linearly varying load, multiplication by the linear shape functions produces quadratic integrands, so two-point quadrature is required for exact integration.
Using more points than necessary can still give an exact result, but requires additional integrand evaluations. Underintegration may reproduce an aggregate quantity, such as the total distributed force, without reproducing the correct element vector.

16.3 Extract point-and-weight data
Unlike the axial-bar files, examples/gauss_legendre_quadrature.jl is a genuinely new S07 file. Create it with this target function:
gauss_legendre_rule(num_points)
num_points is the requested number of Gauss–Legendre points. The function is responsible only for supplying the rule data and returns a vector of (xi_g, w_g) tuples on \([-1,1]\):
one point:  (0.0, 2.0)
two points: (-1 / sqrt(3), 1.0), (1 / sqrt(3), 1.0)
This function stores quadrature-rule data only. It accepts an integer specifying the number of Gauss–Legendre points, currently limited to one or two, and reports an error for any other value.

title: 16  Implementing Gauss–Legendre quadrature for the two-node bar
text:
16.4 First scalar checks
examples/gauss_legendre_scalar_integration.jl is a genuinely new S07 file. Create it and collect the scalar integration examples described below in a plain function with the target interface evaluate_scalar_gauss_legendre_examples(), then call it at top level. The function takes no arguments and returns the four computed results: the one-point result for the linear polynomial, the one- and two-point results for the cubic polynomial, and the mapped two-point result.
Use these examples to make the quadrature process explicit. At every Gauss point, identify xi_g and w_g, evaluate the integrand, form the weighted contribution, and accumulate the result with +=.
Begin by integrating the linear polynomial
\[
  2 + 3\xi
\]
over \([-1,1]\) with the one-point Gauss–Legendre rule. Its exact integral is \(4\). Because the one-point rule has degree of exactness one, it reproduces this result exactly.
Next, integrate the cubic polynomial
\[
  1 - 2\xi + 3\xi^2 + 4\xi^3
\]
over \([-1,1]\) and compare the one- and two-point rules. Its exact integral is also \(4\). The one-point rule is not sufficient because its degree of exactness does not include quadratic and cubic terms. The two-point rule has degree of exactness three and therefore reproduces the exact integral.
Finally, apply the same quadrature procedure to the physical interval \([0,3]\) by integrating \(x^2+1\), whose exact integral is \(12\). Map each Gauss point from the reference interval using
J = (b - a) / 2
x_g = (a + b) / 2 + J * xi_g
The mapping and Jacobian are exact; the numerical approximation enters only through the finite weighted sum used for integration. At each quadrature point, x_g identifies the physical location corresponding to xi_g and is therefore used to evaluate the mapped integrand.
This same reference-to-physical mapping will be used in the two-node bar element. In the present formulation, E_g and A_g are constant and q_g is interpolated from its endpoint values, but x_g is still computed explicitly. Its role becomes essential when material properties, geometry, loading, or recovered fields vary with physical position.






NoteExact quadrature and floating-point arithmetic



The two-point rule is mathematically exact for the mapped quadratic polynomial, but the script may display 12.000000000000002 rather than 12.0. This is ordinary Float64 roundoff from arithmetic and mapping operations. Exact quadrature does not imply bitwise equality in floating-point arithmetic, so the regression tests use isapprox rather than exact == comparison.








TipExercise — From a scalar to a vector contribution



Using the one-point Gauss–Legendre rule, evaluate
\[
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1-\xi\\
  1+\xi
  \end{bmatrix}
  \,d\xi
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2\\
  2
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Initialize a two-entry result vector with zeros. Then loop over the Gauss points and weights. At each point, evaluate the two functions at xi_g and collect them in a two-entry vector, for example
integrand_value = [
    1.0 - xi_g,
    1.0 + xi_g,
]
Multiply this vector by the Gauss weight to obtain the weighted contribution, then accumulate it into the result vector with +=.
The structure is therefore the same as in the scalar examples:
scalar:  integrand value  -> weighted scalar contribution -> scalar result
vector:  integrand vector -> weighted vector contribution -> vector result
Check that the final vector is [2.0, 2.0].
This is the pattern used later for the consistent element load vector. The stiffness matrix follows the same idea, except that the quantity evaluated and accumulated at each Gauss point is a matrix rather than a scalar or vector.
The next step is to apply this Gauss–Legendre accumulation pattern to the two-node bar, for both the element stiffness matrix and the consistent load vector.

text:
16.5 Adapt local bar-array evaluation
Copy examples/axial_bar_fem.jl, rename the copy examples/axial_bar_gauss_legendre_fem.jl, then replace only the closed-form element-evaluation and Gauss-point response-sampling operations. Keep the established assembly, nodal-force, prescribed-displacement, global-solve, and reaction-recovery operations structurally aligned with the original file. This remains a second, explicit two-node axial-bar implementation.
The first target function is:
integrate_two_node_bar_gauss_legendre(x_e, E_e, A_e, q_1, q_2, num_gauss_legendre_points)
Here x_e contains the two physical endpoint coordinates; E_e and A_e are the element material and cross-sectional data; q_1 and q_2 are the endpoint distributed-load values; and num_gauss_legendre_points selects the rule. The function constructs the local stiffness matrix and consistent distributed-load vector, returning K_e, f_e. Equal q_1 and q_2 represent a uniform load; unequal values describe a linearly varying load.
Initialize a \(2\times2\) matrix K_e and a two-entry vector f_e. For each (xi_g, w_g), map xi_g to x_g, evaluate J, construct \(\mathbf N_g\) and \(\mathbf B_g\), use \(E_g=E_e\) and \(A_g=A_e\), and interpolate \(q_g=N_{g,1}q_1+N_{g,2}q_2\). Use explicit local loops to accumulate:
\[
  K_{e,ij}\mathrel{+}=w_gB_{g,i}E_gA_gB_{g,j}J,
  \qquad
  f_{e,i}\mathrel{+}=w_gN_{g,i}q_gJ.
\]
Use one quadrature loop. At each Gauss–Legendre point:

map xi_g to the physical element and compute J;
evaluate N_g and B_g;
evaluate the element data needed at that point;
compute the contribution to each entry of K_e and add it to the current value;
compute the contribution to each entry of f_e and add it to the current value.

Keep these steps explicit in the code:
for (xi_g, w_g) in gauss_legendre_rule(num_gauss_legendre_points)
    # Map xi_g to the physical element and compute J.
    # Evaluate N_g and B_g.
    # Evaluate the element data at this point.
    # Compute and add the contribution to K_e.
    # Compute and add the contribution to f_e.
end
The closed-form implementation keeps bar_stiffness(...) and bar_distributed_load(...) as conceptually separate element contributions. In the Gauss–Legendre implementation, integrate_two_node_bar_gauss_legendre(...) constructs both K_e and f_e inside one quadrature loop because both contributions use the same points, weights, affine mapping, and Jacobian. The stiffness and consistent distributed-load accumulations remain visibly separate within that loop.
Computing both K_e and f_e in the same quadrature loop does not mean that the matrix and vector are the same mathematical object. They remain distinct element quantities, but their evaluation follows the same sequence at each Gauss point: mapping, evaluation of the required quantities, weighting, and accumulation. Keeping these closely related operations together is consistent with the Single Responsibility Principle: one coherent responsibility does not have to consist of only one small calculation.

16.6 Check special cases
For constant \(E_e\) and \(A_e\), one point gives exactly:
\[
  \mathbf K_e=\frac{E_eA_e}{L_e}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For uniform \(q_e\), one point also gives exactly:
\[
  \mathbf f_e^q=\frac{q_eL_e}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Compare quadrature arrays with these closed-form references. For \(L_e=3\), \(q_1=2\), and \(q_2=8\), both rules give resultant \(15\). One point gives \([7.5,7.5]^{\mathsf T}\), but two points give the exact consistent distribution \([6,9]^{\mathsf T}\). A correct resultant is not the same as an exact nodal distribution.

16.7 Adapt assembly and solution
Next adapt the corresponding closed-form functions. Use these target interfaces:
assemble_axial_bar_gauss_legendre!(
    K,
    f,
    node_coordinates,
    element_connectivity,

This ordering follows the dependencies of the implementation: the axial-bar functions use the shared assembly operations and the Gauss–Legendre rule. title: 16  Implementing Gauss–Legendre quadrature for the two-node bar
text:
16.9 Recover responses at Gauss points
The Gauss–Legendre implementation uses a separate response-recovery function from the closed-form implementation:
recover_axial_bar_response_gauss_legendre(
    node_coordinates,
    element_connectivity,
    element_E,
    element_A,
    u,
    num_gauss_legendre_points,
)
The function receives the mesh, element material and cross-sectional data, the computed global displacement vector, and the response-sampling rule. For each element and each point from that rule, evaluate xi_g, x_g, the shape functions, B_g, and then compute
\[
  \varepsilon_g=\mathbf B_g\mathbf u_e,
  \qquad
  \sigma_g=E_g\varepsilon_g,
  \qquad
  N_g=A_g\sigma_g.
\]
These are response samples at physical Gauss-point locations, not quadrature integrals. Do not multiply strain, stress, or axial force by a weight or by the Jacobian, and do not accumulate them. The function returns simple element-by- Gauss-point arrays for the reference coordinates, physical coordinates, strain, stress, and axial force, in that order:
gauss_point_reference_coordinates,
gauss_point_coordinates,
gauss_point_strain,
gauss_point_stress,
gauss_point_axial_force
For this two-node linear bar with constant E and A, strain, stress, and axial force are constant within an element. The finite element response sampled at the two Gauss points of a single element therefore has the same value. This, however, does not make the finite element response exact at every sampled location. In fact, the exact axial force varies linearly within each element under the uniform distributed load, so its values at the two physical Gauss-point coordinates are generally different. Therefore, evaluating the same linear-element response at more points does not increase its interpolation order or improve its accuracy.
The one-point benchmark is a special case. Its Gauss–Legendre point has xi = 0, which maps to the physical midpoint of an affine two-node element. The previously established midpoint agreement is therefore recovered when the response is sampled at one point. With two sampling points, instead, the finite element axial force remains constant within the element, while the exact axial force is generally different at the two physical locations.
The concentrated force introduces a separate consideration. Since the force is applied at a mesh node, the jump in the exact derivative occurs at the boundary between two elements. Each element therefore lies within one smooth branch of the exact solution, and its interior Gauss points do not sample across the discontinuity. This does not, however, make the finite element derivative exact throughout the element.






TipExercise — Change from one to two Gauss points



The four-element benchmark deliberately uses num_gauss_legendre_points = 1: one point already integrates the current constant-property stiffness and uniform distributed-load contributions exactly. Change only this setting to 2, adapt the output if necessary so that all relevant results are displayed, run the benchmark again, and investigate the following questions before drawing conclusions.
For element integration and construction:

Do the global displacement vector and support reaction change?
Do the element stiffness matrices change?
Do the consistent distributed-load vectors change for the current uniform q?
What do the polynomial degrees of the present integrands say about the required quadrature order?

For response sampling and post-processing:

How many response locations now occur in each element?
What are their reference coordinates, and where do they map in physical space?
Are the two finite element strains, stresses, and axial forces in one element different? Why or why not?

Finally, evaluate the exact axial force at both physical Gauss-point coordinates. How do those values compare with the two sampled finite element axial forces? Explain what changed by using two points: numerical-integration accuracy, the finite element approximation space, the number of response sampling locations, or some combination of these. Relate your answer to the one-point case, where \(\xi_g=0\) maps to the midpoint and gives the previously observed midpoint agreement.

text:
16.10 Verify the Gauss–Legendre implementation
The S07 regression tests are supplied reference material, not a student coding task in this chapter. After completing the implementation, study test/runtests.jl to see how the expected numerical behavior is turned into automated regression checks.
Focus on what each group of tests protects:

previously accepted MiniFEM results that must remain unchanged;
the Gauss–Legendre point-and-weight rules and their expected degree of exactness;
mapped scalar integration;
agreement with the closed-form element stiffness matrix and consistent load vector where exact reference results are available;
the different behavior of one- and two-point quadrature for a linearly varying distributed load;
the displacement, support reaction, and Gauss-point response values of the four-element benchmark.

Notice also how the tests use isapprox for floating-point comparisons rather than requiring bitwise equality.
The four-element regression test deliberately uses different numbers of Gauss–Legendre points for element integration and response sampling. The global finite element solution is computed with one Gauss point, as in the reference benchmark:
num_gauss_legendre_points = 1
After the displacement solution has been obtained, the response is sampled separately at two Gauss points per element:
recover_axial_bar_response_gauss_legendre(..., 2)
The two points used for response sampling do not recompute the global solution. They only provide two locations at which the already-computed finite element response is evaluated. The tests then verify that strain, stress, and axial force have the same finite element value at both locations within each linear bar element, even though the exact axial force generally has different values at the two corresponding physical coordinates.
This distinction is important: the number of Gauss points used for element integration and the number of points used for response sampling need not be the same.
The tests are a worked example of regression-test design. They turn analytical results and previously verified numerical behavior into automated checks that can be rerun after later changes to the code. Regression tests protect accepted behavior: they do not replace independent analytical verification or physical validation.
Run:
julia test/runtests.jl
julia examples/gauss_legendre_scalar_integration.jl
julia examples/four_element_axial_bar.jl
julia examples/four_element_axial_bar_gauss_legendre.jl

text:
16.11 Reflection and what comes next
The closed-form and Gauss–Legendre implementations describe the same two-node bar element. They differ only in how the element stiffness matrix and consistent load vector are evaluated. Keeping both implementations available makes their differences easy to compare and prepares for later problems in which closed-form integration is no longer practical.

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.1 Interpolation, mapping, and numerical integration
The preceding chapters introduced several ideas that now work together in a finite element calculation.
In Chapter 13, Gauss–Legendre quadrature was defined on the standard interval
\[
  -1\leq\xi\leq1.
\]
In Chapter 14, an exact coordinate transformation was used to relate this standard interval to a physical interval. For a two-node bar element, this gave the mapping
\[
  x=x(\xi),
\]
the Jacobian
\[
  J=\frac{dx}{d\xi},
\]
the differential transformation
\[
  dx=J\,d\xi,
\]
and the derivative transformation
\[
  \frac{d}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}\frac{d}{d\xi}.
\]
Finally, Chapter 15 combined these operations to evaluate the stiffness matrix and consistent distributed-load vector of the two-node bar on the standard interval.
We can now step back from those individual operations and recognize the more general finite element construction that connects them. This construction is called the isoparametric formulation.
The central idea is simple: the same shape functions defined on a reference domain are used to interpolate both the geometry of the physical element and the primary unknown field. The coordinate mapping, its Jacobian, the transformation of derivatives, and the element integrals then follow from this common description.
The two-node bar considered so far already has this isoparametric structure. In this chapter, we make that structure explicit and generalize it to a one-dimensional element with \(n\) nodes. We will distinguish between interpolation of the displacement field, interpolation of the geometry, and numerical integration, and we will show how these operations are connected through the Jacobian of the coordinate mapping.
The two-node bar remains the main concrete example. Higher-order interpolation is introduced only to examine an important feature of the geometry mapping: while the two-node mapping is affine and has a constant Jacobian, a higher-order mapping can be non-affine and have a Jacobian that varies within the element. This also provides a natural setting in which to discuss the validity of the coordinate mapping.
The full development of the three-node quadratic bar is deferred to the next chapter. There we will construct its quadratic shape functions systematically and use the isoparametric framework developed here to derive its finite element equations.
Three operations that appear together in an element calculation should first be kept conceptually distinct.
The global finite element displacement field is represented within each element through interpolation of the nodal displacement values:
\[
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
When working within an element, we will often write \(u^h(\xi)\) as a shorthand for \(u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)\).
Here, \(\mathbf{u}_e\) collects the global nodal displacement values associated with the nodes of element \(e\). Neighboring elements therefore do not define independent displacement fields: they provide local representations of the same global finite element field and share the displacement values at common nodes.
The physical position is obtained through a coordinate mapping:
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{x}_e.
\]
An integral on the standard interval may then be evaluated by numerical integration:
\[
  \int_{-1}^{1}h(\xi)\,d\xi
  \approx
  \sum_{g=1}^{n_g}w_g h(\xi_g).
\]
These three operations interact, but they have different purposes:
The isoparametric formulation defines how the geometry and displacement field are represented. The resulting element integrals may then be evaluated analytically or numerically, for example using Gauss–Legendre quadrature.
The distinction established previously between an exact coordinate transformation and numerical quadrature therefore remains unchanged. The mapping and the transformations derived from it are exact for the geometry represented by the finite element. Approximation by quadrature enters only when an integral is replaced by a finite weighted sum.

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.2 The familiar two-node element revisited
Consider a two-node element occupying the physical interval
\[
  x_1 \leq x \leq x_2.
\]
To describe this element in standard coordinates, we introduce the reference interval
\[
  -1 \leq \xi \leq 1,
\]
with the two local nodes located at
\[
  \xi_1=-1,
  \qquad
  \xi_2=1.
\]
The coordinate mapping relates each point \(\xi\) in the reference interval to the corresponding physical position \(x\) in the element.
The two-node shape functions on the reference interval are
\[
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1-\xi}{2},
  \qquad
  N_2(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1+\xi}{2}.
\]
Using these shape functions, the displacement field within the element is interpolated from the nodal displacements as
\[
  \boxed{
  u^h(\xi)
  =
  N_1(\xi)u_1
  +
  N_2(\xi)u_2.
  }
\]
The same shape functions are also used to map the reference coordinate \(\xi\) to the physical position \(x\):
\[
  \boxed{
  x(\xi)
  =
  N_1(\xi)x_1
  +
  N_2(\xi)x_2.
  }
\]
The two expressions therefore have the same interpolation structure. In the first, the shape functions interpolate the nodal displacement values \(u_1\) and \(u_2\); in the second, they interpolate the nodal coordinates \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
Using the same shape functions to represent both the geometry and the displacement field is the essential idea of the isoparametric formulation. The two-node bar introduced earlier already has this structure, even though we had not yet identified it explicitly as isoparametric.

17.2.1 The same interpolation viewed in different coordinates
The connection can also be seen by starting with the familiar two-node shape functions written directly in the physical coordinate. For an element with \(x_2>x_1\),
\[
  N_1(x)
  =
  \frac{x_2-x}{x_2-x_1},
  \qquad
  N_2(x)
  =
  \frac{x-x_1}{x_2-x_1}.
\]
The exact affine mapping established in Chapter 14 is
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}
  +
  \frac{x_2-x_1}{2}\xi.
\]
Substituting this expression for \(x\) into the first physical-coordinate shape function gives
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  N_1(x(\xi))
  &=
  \frac{
  x_2-
  \left[
  \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}
  +
  \dfrac{x_2-x_1}{2}\xi
  \right]
  }
  {x_2-x_1}
  \\[2mm]
  &=
  \frac{1-\xi}{2}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
Similarly,
\[
  N_2(x(\xi))
  =
  \frac{1+\xi}{2}.
\]
Thus the shape functions expressed in terms of the reference coordinate are not unrelated new functions. They describe the same nodal interpolation after the coordinate change.
The advantage of the reference-domain description becomes much greater for higher-order and multidimensional elements: instead of deriving a new set of shape functions directly in physical coordinates for every element geometry, we define the interpolation once on a simple reference domain and use a mapping to describe each physical element.

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
section: 17.3 Nodal interpolation and Lagrange shape functions
text:
17.3 Nodal interpolation and Lagrange shape functions
The shape functions used so far have the nodal interpolation property
\[
  \boxed{
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij},
  }
\]
where the Kronecker delta is
\[
  \delta_{ij}
  =
  \begin{cases}
  1, & i=j,\\
  0, & i\neq j.
  \end{cases}
\]
For example,
\[
  N_1(-1)=1,
  \qquad
  N_1(1)=0,
\]
and
\[
  N_2(-1)=0,
  \qquad
  N_2(1)=1.
\]
Each shape function therefore takes the value one at its own node and zero at the other node.
Polynomial interpolation functions constructed to satisfy this nodal property are Lagrange interpolation functions. The two shape functions already used for the linear bar are the degree-one Lagrange shape functions associated with the two reference nodes \(\xi=-1\) and \(\xi=1\).
The terms Lagrange and isoparametric describe different aspects of the formulation:

Lagrange interpolation concerns the construction and nodal interpolation property of the shape functions;
Isoparametric formulation concerns how those shape functions are used: the same interpolation functions describe both the element geometry and the primary unknown field.

Higher-order Lagrange shape functions will be constructed explicitly when the three-node quadratic bar element is introduced.

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.4 The isoparametric concept
Consider a one-dimensional reference domain with \(n\) local nodes located at
\[
  \xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_n.
\]
Let
\[
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  N_1(\xi)
  &
  N_2(\xi)
  &
  \cdots
  &
  N_n(\xi)
  \end{bmatrix}
\]
collect the shape functions defined on this reference domain.
The physical nodal coordinates are collected in
\[
  \mathbf{x}_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  x_1\\
  x_2\\
  \vdots\\
  x_n
  \end{bmatrix},
\]
while the nodal displacement values are
\[
  \mathbf{u}_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_2\\
  \vdots\\
  u_n
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The geometry is interpolated as
\[
  \boxed{
  x(\xi)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{x}_e
  =
  \sum_{i=1}^{n}N_i(\xi)x_i,
  }
\]
and the displacement field is interpolated as
\[
  \boxed{
  u^h(\xi)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{u}_e
  =
  \sum_{i=1}^{n}N_i(\xi)u_i.
  }
\]
A finite element formulation is isoparametric when the same shape functions, defined on the reference domain, are used to interpolate both the element geometry and the primary unknown field.
For the one-dimensional bar considered here, the same \(N_i(\xi)\) interpolate the physical coordinate \(x\) from the nodal coordinates \(x_i\) and the displacement \(u^h\) from the nodal displacements \(u_i\).
The two interpolations therefore have the same mathematical structure but act on different nodal quantities. This common structure is illustrated in Figure 17.1.






Figure 17.1: The same shape functions \(\mathbf{N}(\xi)\), defined on the reference domain, interpolate both the physical geometry from the nodal coordinates \(\mathbf{x}_e\) and the displacement field from the nodal values \(\mathbf{u}_e\).

17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.5 The reference-to-physical map
The expression
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{x}_e
\]
should be understood as a map from the reference domain to the physical element:
\[
  \boxed{
  [-1,1]
  \longrightarrow
  \Omega_e.
  }
\]
A position \(\xi\) in the reference domain determines a physical position
\[
  x=x(\xi)
\]
through the nodal coordinates and the shape functions defined on the reference domain.
For a valid one-dimensional element, the mapping must describe the physical element without collapsing or folding it. In particular, distinct positions in the reference domain should correspond to distinct physical positions.
For the two-node element with \(x_2>x_1\), the mapping is
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}
  +
  \frac{x_2-x_1}{2}\xi,
\]
which is one-to-one and preserves the ordering of points:
\[
  \xi_a<\xi_b
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  x(\xi_a)<x(\xi_b).
\]
This familiar affine case is the simplest example of the more general isoparametric mapping.

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
section: 17.6 The Jacobian follows from the geometry
text:
17.6 The Jacobian follows from the geometry
The geometry of the element is described by the interpolation
\[
  x(\xi) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} N_i(\xi)\,x_i.
\]
Differentiating this mapping with respect to the reference coordinate gives
\[
  \frac{dx}{d\xi} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{dN_i}{d\xi}\,x_i,
\]
which, as introduced in Chapter 14, is precisely the Jacobian of the one-dimensional mapping:
\[
  J(\xi) = \frac{dx}{d\xi} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{dN_i}{d\xi}\,x_i,
\]
or, in matrix form,
\[
  \boxed{
    J(\xi) = \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}\,\mathbf{x}_e.
  }
\]
The Jacobian is thus fixed entirely by two ingredients: the shape functions used to interpolate the geometry, and the physical nodal coordinates.
For the two-node element the shape-function derivatives are constant,
\[
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi} = \begin{bmatrix} -1/2 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix},
\]
and substituting into the expression of the Jacobian gives
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    J
    &= \begin{bmatrix} -1/2 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}
       \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \\[1mm]
    &= \frac{x_2 - x_1}{2} = \frac{L_e}{2}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
Because the geometry interpolation is linear in \(\xi\), the coordinate mapping is affine. Its derivative, and therefore the Jacobian, is constant over the element:
\[
  J=\frac{L_e}{2}.
\]
The general isoparametric expression therefore recovers the result obtained earlier for the affine two-node mapping.

17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.7 Transforming derivatives through the mapping
The derivative transformation used in the preceding chapters can now be derived directly from the isoparametric mapping.
Consider a scalar field written in physical coordinates as
\[
  u=u(x).
\]
Because
\[
  x=x(\xi),
\]
the same field can be viewed as the composition
\[
  u=u(x(\xi)).
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\xi\) and applying the chain rule gives
\[
  \frac{du}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{du}{dx}
  \frac{dx}{d\xi}.
\]
Since
\[
  J=\frac{dx}{d\xi},
\]
we obtain
\[
  \frac{du}{d\xi}
  =
  J\frac{du}{dx}.
\]
Provided that \(J\neq0\),
\[
  \boxed{
  \frac{du}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{du}{d\xi}.
  }
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \boxed{
  \frac{d}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d}{d\xi}.
  }
\]
This relation is not an additional approximation. It follows exactly from the coordinate mapping and the chain rule.

17.7.1 Derivatives of the shape functions
Within an element, the finite element displacement field can be represented in terms of the reference coordinate as
\[
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
Differentiating this representation with respect to \(\xi\) gives
\[
  \frac{d u^h(x(\xi))}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
The axial strain, however, is defined in terms of the derivative with respect to the physical coordinate \(x\) as
\[
  \varepsilon^h(x)
  =
  \frac{du^h}{dx}.
\]
Using the chain rule,
\[
  \frac{d u^h(x(\xi))}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{du^h}{dx}
  \frac{dx}{d\xi}
  =
  J(\xi)\frac{du^h}{dx}.
\]
Therefore, equating the two expressions for the derivative with respect to \(\xi\) gives
\[
  \frac{du^h}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J(\xi)}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
The derivatives of the shape functions with respect to the physical coordinate are therefore obtained from their derivatives on the reference domain through the Jacobian. Defining the strain–displacement matrix as
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1}{J(\xi)}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi},
  }
\]
the physical strain field can be evaluated in terms of the reference coordinate as
\[
  \boxed{
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)\mathbf{u}_e.
  }
\]
The strain remains a field defined in physical space; the reference coordinate \(\xi\) is used to evaluate it through the coordinate mapping \(x=x(\xi)\). This is also what happens in the finite element implementation: the strain is typically evaluated at a Gauss point specified by its reference coordinate \(\xi_g\). The shape-function derivatives and the Jacobian are evaluated directly at \(\xi_g\), giving
\[
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi_g)\right)
  =
  \mathbf{B}(\xi_g)\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
It is therefore not necessary to first compute the physical coordinate \(x(\xi_g)\) merely to evaluate the strain there. The mapping identifies which physical point of the element corresponds to the Gauss-point location \(\xi_g\in[-1,1]\), while the isoparametric expressions allow the required quantities to be evaluated directly in terms of \(\xi_g\).
This transformation is one of the main practical advantages of the reference description as it avoids the need to construct separate explicit expressions for \(N_i(x)\) for each physical element. The shape functions and their derivatives are defined in terms of \(\xi\), and the Jacobian transforms the derivatives required with respect to the physical coordinate \(x\).

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
section: 17.9 Element integrals on the reference domain
text:
17.9 Element integrals on the reference domain
The element stiffness matrix of the two-node bar element is
\[
  \mathbf{K}_e
  =
  \int_{\Omega_e}
  \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}
  EA
  \mathbf{B}
  \,dx
\]
which, using the isoparametric mapping, can be expressed over the reference domain as
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf{K}_e
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  E\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  A\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  \mathbf{B}(\xi)
  J(\xi)
  \,d\xi.
  }
\]
The same transformation applies to the consistent distributed-load vector,
\[
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  =
  \int_{\Omega_e}
  \mathbf{N}^{\mathsf T}q\,dx,
\]
which becomes
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf{N}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  q\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  J(\xi)
  \,d\xi.
  }
\]
These are the same expressions used in Chapter 15. The difference is that we now interpret them as consequences of the general isoparametric construction rather than as relations specific to the affine two-node element.
If numerical integration is used,
\[
  \mathbf{K}_e
  \approx
  \sum_{g=1}^{n_g}
  w_g
  \mathbf{B}_g^{\mathsf T}
  E_gA_g
  \mathbf{B}_g
  J_g
\]
and
\[
  \mathbf{f}_e^q
  \approx
  \sum_{g=1}^{n_g}
  w_g
  \mathbf{N}_g^{\mathsf T}
  q_g
  J_g,
\]
where
\[
  \mathbf{N}_g
  =
  \mathbf{N}(\xi_g),
  \qquad
  \mathbf{B}_g
  =
  \mathbf{B}(\xi_g),
  \qquad
  J_g
  =
  J(\xi_g).
\]
The notation \(J_g\) is useful in the general case because the Jacobian need not be constant over the element.

17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.10 Interpolation order and quadrature order
The preceding Gauss–Legendre chapter established that the minimum exact quadrature rule is determined by the degree of each complete transformed scalar integrand.
The isoparametric formulation shows how the different contributions to that integrand arise from the interpolation, the geometry mapping, and the physical data. Suppose, for example, that the shape functions are quadratic in \(\xi\). Then
\[
  N_i(\xi)
\]
has polynomial degree two, while
\[
  \frac{dN_i}{d\xi}
\]
has degree one.
For an affine geometry mapping with constant \(J\), a representative transformed integrand containing two shape functions is
\[
  N_i(\xi)N_j(\xi)J.
\]
If the shape functions are quadratic in \(\xi\), this integrand has degree four.
Exact Gauss–Legendre integration therefore requires three points because
\[
  4\leq2(3)-1=5.
\]
A stiffness integrand for constant \(E\), constant \(A\), and constant \(J\) contains
\[
  B_iEA B_jJ.
\]
Since
\[
  B_i
  =
  \frac{1}{J}\frac{dN_i}{d\xi},
\]
each \(B_i\) is linear when \(J\) is constant. The stiffness integrand is therefore quadratic:
\[
  1+1=2,
\]
and a two-point Gauss–Legendre rule is sufficient for exact integration.
Thus the same quadratic interpolation can produce element integrands requiring different numbers of integration points.
The interpolation order alone does not determine the quadrature order.






ImportantSelect quadrature from the transformed integrand



The number of Gauss–Legendre points must be selected from the complete scalar integrand after the coordinate and derivative transformations have been performed.
Neither the polynomial degree of the shape functions alone nor the degree of one individual factor is sufficient.

17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.11 Affine and non-affine isoparametric mappings
For the two-node bar considered so far, the geometry interpolation produces the affine mapping introduced in Chapter 14:
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}
  +
  \frac{L_e}{2}\xi,
\]
with constant Jacobian
\[
  J
  =
  \frac{dx}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{L_e}{2}.
\]
In that case, the local scale factor between the reference and physical coordinates is the same everywhere in the element.
The isoparametric formulation, however, is not restricted to affine mappings. When higher-order shape functions are used to interpolate the geometry, the map \(x(\xi)\) can become non-affine and the Jacobian can vary with \(\xi\). Higher-order interpolation does not, however, make the mapping non-affine automatically: this depends on the physical positions of the element nodes.
To illustrate this distinction, we briefly consider a three-node geometry. The purpose here is only to examine the coordinate mapping \(x(\xi)\) and its Jacobian. The three-node quadratic bar element itself will be developed in the next chapter.
Consider the reference interval
\[
  -1\leq\xi\leq1,
\]
with three local nodes located at
\[
  \xi_1=-1,
  \qquad
  \xi_2=0,
  \qquad
  \xi_3=1,
\]
and quadratic nodal shape functions
\[
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1}{2}\xi(\xi-1),
\]
\[
  N_2(\xi)
  =
  1-\xi^2,
\]
and
\[
  N_3(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1}{2}\xi(\xi+1).
\]
Their construction will be derived in the following chapter. Here they are used only to examine the geometry mapping
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  N_1(\xi)x_1
  +
  N_2(\xi)x_2
  +
  N_3(\xi)x_3.
\]

17.11.1 A three-node geometry with a midpoint node
Let the physical nodal coordinates be
\[
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=\frac{L_e}{2},
  \qquad
  x_3=L_e.
\]
The middle node is exactly halfway between the two end nodes. The isoparametric mapping becomes
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  x(\xi)
  &=
  N_1(\xi)\,0
  +
  N_2(\xi)\frac{L_e}{2}
  +
  N_3(\xi)L_e
  \\[1mm]
  &=
  \frac{L_e}{2}(1+\xi).
  \end{aligned}
\]
Although quadratic shape functions were used to interpolate the geometry, the quadratic terms cancel. The actual coordinate mapping is affine.
Its Jacobian is therefore constant:
\[
  \boxed{
  J
  =
  \frac{dx}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{L_e}{2}.
  }
\]
This distinction is important:

The interpolation used to describe the geometry may be quadratic even when the resulting physical mapping happens to be affine.

The word isoparametric describes the relationship between geometry and field interpolation. It does not imply that the resulting geometry mapping must be non-affine.


17.11.2 Moving the middle node
Now consider the unit physical interval with
\[
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=0.6,
  \qquad
  x_3=1.
\]
The middle physical node no longer lies at the midpoint \(x=0.5\).
Using the same quadratic shape functions,
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  x(\xi)
  &=
  N_1(\xi)\,0
  +
  N_2(\xi)\,0.6
  +
  N_3(\xi)\,1
  \\[1mm]
  &=
  0.6+0.5\xi-0.1\xi^2.
  \end{aligned}
\]
The quadratic term no longer cancels. The mapping is genuinely non-affine.
Its Jacobian is
\[
  \boxed{
  J(\xi)
  =
  0.5-0.2\xi.
  }
\]
The local scale factor therefore varies through the element.
For
\[
  -1\leq\xi\leq1,
\]
the Jacobian ranges between
\[
  J(-1)=0.7
\]
and
\[
  J(1)=0.3.
\]
It remains positive throughout the element, so the mapping remains valid even though it is non-affine.

17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.12 Mapping validity and the Jacobian
The Jacobian is not only an integration factor. It also provides information about the validity of the element geometry.
For an orientation-preserving one-dimensional mapping, we require
\[
  \boxed{
  J(\xi)>0
  \qquad
  \text{for all }
  -1\leq\xi\leq1.
  }
\]
If
\[
  J(\xi)=0
\]
at some position, the mapping becomes locally singular: the local scale factor between reference and physical coordinates vanishes at that position.
If
\[
  J(\xi)<0,
\]
the local orientation is reversed.
A mapping whose Jacobian changes sign within the reference domain cannot provide the required one-to-one, orientation-preserving description of the physical element.
For the affine two-node element with \(x_2>x_1\),
\[
  J=\frac{x_2-x_1}{2}>0
\]
automatically.
For higher-order geometry, however,
\[
  J=J(\xi)
\]
may vary, and its behavior must be considered throughout the element.
The displaced-middle-node example above gives
\[
  J(\xi)=0.5-0.2\xi,
\]
which remains positive on the entire reference interval. It therefore illustrates an important distinction:

A non-affine mapping is not necessarily an invalid mapping.

The relevant question is whether the mapping remains one-to-one and orientation-preserving, with \(J(\xi)>0\) throughout the reference domain.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.13 Non-affine mappings and quadrature
A variable Jacobian also affects the form of transformed element integrands.
For the axial-bar stiffness,
\[
  \mathbf{B}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}
  EA
  \mathbf{B}
  J
  &=
  \left(
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}
  \right)^{\mathsf T}
  EA
  \left(
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}
  \right)
  J
  \\[2mm]
  &=
  \frac{EA}{J}
  \left(
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}
  \right)^{\mathsf T}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
When \(J\) is constant, polynomial degree counting is straightforward.
When
\[
  J=J(\xi)
\]
varies, the factor
\[
  \frac{1}{J(\xi)}
\]
must be included in the complete transformed integrand. Even when the shape functions are polynomial, the stiffness integrand may therefore no longer be a polynomial.
In that case, the Gauss–Legendre degree-of-exactness rule
\[
  p\leq2n_g-1
\]
does not provide a finite polynomial degree from which exactness can be guaranteed. Numerical integration remains applicable, but its accuracy must be assessed rather than inferred from polynomial degree alone.
This is why the quadrature rule must always be selected by examining the complete transformed integrand.
The first three-node bar developed in the next chapter will deliberately place the middle node at the physical midpoint. Its mapping therefore remains affine and its Jacobian constant, allowing the effects of quadratic displacement interpolation to be studied without simultaneously introducing the additional complications of a variable geometric mapping.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.14 Isoparametric and other parametric formulations
The formulation considered throughout this chapter uses the same interpolation functions for the geometry and the displacement field and is therefore isoparametric.
Other choices are possible. If the geometry is interpolated with a lower polynomial order than the primary field, the formulation is called subparametric; if the geometry uses a higher order, it is called superparametric.
These alternatives are not needed for the developments that follow. We will continue with the isoparametric formulation so that the same reference shape functions retain a clear and consistent role in both the geometry and the unknown field.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension

title: 17  The isoparametric formulation in one dimension
text:
17.15 What comes next
The isoparametric framework is now in place: the same shape functions describe the element geometry and the displacement field, the Jacobian connects reference and physical coordinates, and the resulting element integrals can be evaluated on the reference domain.
The next chapter applies this framework to the three-node quadratic bar. There, the additional node supports a quadratic displacement interpolation, allowing the strain field to vary within an element. We will construct the corresponding Lagrange shape functions and use them to derive the element equations, numerical integration, and response recovery.






TipExercises




For the two-node interpolation on the reference interval, verify directly that
\[
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}
\]
for all four combinations of \(i\) and \(j\). Explain why this property makes \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) the values of the interpolated displacement at the two element nodes.
Starting from
\[
  x(\xi)=\mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{x}_e,
\]
derive
\[
  J(\xi)
  =
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}\mathbf{x}_e.
\]
Identify which quantities determine the Jacobian and which common finite element quantities do not enter this expression.
Starting from
\[
  u^h=u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right),
\]
use the chain rule to derive
\[
  \frac{du^h}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{du^h}{d\xi}.
\]
Explain why this relation is part of the exact coordinate transformation rather than a numerical approximation.
Let \(N_i(x)\) and \(N_j(x)\) denote shape functions expressed in the physical coordinate, and let \(\bar N_i(\xi)\) and \(\bar N_j(\xi)\) denote their representations on the reference domain. Consider
\[
  I_N
  =
  \int_{\Omega_e}N_i(x)N_j(x)\,dx
\]
and
\[
  I_B
  =
  \int_{\Omega_e}
  \frac{dN_i}{dx}
  \frac{dN_j}{dx}
  \,dx.
\]
Transform both integrals to the reference coordinate and identify every factor of \(J\) and \(1/J\). Explain why the two transformed integrands contain the Jacobian differently.
Suppose that \(\bar N_i(\xi)\) and \(\bar N_j(\xi)\) are quadratic and \(J\) is constant. Determine the polynomial degree of
\[
  \bar N_i\bar N_jJ
\]
and the minimum Gauss–Legendre rule required for exact integration.
Then let
\[
  B_i=\frac{dN_i}{dx},
  \qquad
  B_j=\frac{dN_j}{dx},
\]
and repeat the calculation for
\[
  B_iB_jJ
\]
when \(B_i\) and \(B_j\) are linear.
For a quadratic geometry with
\[
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=\frac12,
  \qquad
  x_3=1,
\]
substitute the three quadratic shape functions into
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  \sum_{i=1}^{3}N_i(\xi)x_i
\]
and verify that the quadratic terms cancel. Compute the Jacobian and confirm that the resulting map is affine.
Repeat the preceding calculation for
\[
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=0.6,
  \qquad
  x_3=1.
\]
Verify that
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  0.6+0.5\xi-0.1\xi^2
\]
and
\[
  J(\xi)
  =
  0.5-0.2\xi.
\]
Determine the minimum and maximum values of \(J\) over \(-1\leq\xi\leq1\) and explain why this non-affine mapping remains valid.
Explain the distinction between each of the following pairs of concepts:

isoparametric formulation and numerical integration;
higher-order geometry interpolation and non-affine mapping;
interpolation order and quadrature order;
variable Jacobian and invalid mapping.










ImportantKey points to remember




The isoparametric formulation organizes several ideas introduced in the preceding chapters: interpolation on a reference domain, coordinate mapping, Jacobian transformations, and the transformation and evaluation of element integrals.
Interpolation, coordinate mapping, and numerical integration are distinct operations. The mapping and its derivative transformations are exact for the element geometry being represented; numerical approximation by quadrature begins only when an integral is replaced by a finite quadrature sum.
Lagrange shape functions satisfy the nodal interpolation property
\[
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}.
\]
The two-node bar shape functions already used in the book are linear Lagrange shape functions.
In an isoparametric formulation, the same shape functions defined on the reference domain interpolate both the geometry and the primary unknown field:
\[
  x(\xi)=\mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{x}_e,
  \qquad
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)=\mathbf{N}(\xi)\mathbf{u}_e.
\]
The Jacobian is determined by the geometry:
\[
  J(\xi)
  =
  \frac{dx}{d\xi}
  =
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}\mathbf{x}_e.
\]
Shape-function values and physical derivatives enter the coordinate transformation differently. Differential lengths introduce \(J\), while physical derivatives introduce \(1/J\) through
\[
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{dx}
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{d\xi}.
\]
The number of Gauss–Legendre points must be selected from the complete transformed scalar integrand. Interpolation order alone is not sufficient.
Higher-order geometry interpolation does not necessarily produce a non-affine map. For a three-node geometry whose middle node lies at the physical midpoint, the quadratic geometry interpolation reduces to an affine mapping.
A non-affine mapping can still be valid. In one dimension, an orientation-preserving mapping requires
\[
  J(\xi)>0
\]
throughout the reference domain.
When \(J(\xi)\) varies, factors such as \(1/J(\xi)\) may make a transformed stiffness integrand non-polynomial. The polynomial degree-of-exactness rule then no longer guarantees exact integration with a prescribed finite Gauss–Legendre rule.

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.1 Quadratic shape functions
This chapter develops the three-node quadratic axial-bar element as the first higher-order extension of the two-node bar introduced earlier.
The finite element procedure developed in the previous chapters does not change. We will still interpolate the displacement field, map the reference element to physical space, transform derivatives through the Jacobian, construct and integrate the element equations, assemble the global problem, and recover the element response.
What changes is one fundamental ingredient: the approximation space used within each element.
The two-node axial-bar element uses a linear displacement interpolation,
\[
  u^h\in\mathcal P_1,
\]
and therefore produces a constant strain within each element. Introducing a third node allows the displacement approximation to be enriched to \(u^h\in\mathcal P_2\). For the regular affine element considered in this chapter, this gives \(\varepsilon^h\in\mathcal P_1\).
This change has consequences throughout the element formulation. The strain–displacement matrix is no longer constant, strain and stress can vary within the element, and the polynomial degrees of the stiffness and load integrands change, affecting the quadrature required for exact integration.
At the same time, increasing the interpolation order does not imply that every finite element solution must be quadratic. The approximation spaces are nested,
\[
  \mathcal P_0
  \subset
  \mathcal P_1
  \subset
  \mathcal P_2,
\]
so a quadratic element can also represent constant and linear displacement fields. This connection between the approximation space and the fields that an element can represent exactly will be one of the main themes of the chapter.
We will construct the quadratic Lagrange shape functions, specialize the one-dimensional isoparametric formulation to a regular three-node bar, derive its stiffness matrix and consistent distributed-load vector, and then use two simple one-element problems to examine what the richer approximation space can actually represent.
To construct the quadratic approximation
\[
  u^h\in\mathcal P_2,
\]
consider the reference interval
\[
  -1\le\xi\le1
\]
with three interpolation nodes,
\[
  \xi_1=-1,
  \qquad
  \xi_2=0,
  \qquad
  \xi_3=1.
\]
The corresponding element displacement vector is
\[
  \mathbf u_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
As for the two-node element, the shape functions must satisfy the nodal interpolation conditions
\[
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Let us derive the first shape function directly from these conditions. Since \(N_1\) is quadratic, it can be expressed as the quadratic polynomial
\[
  N_1(\xi)=a+b\xi+c\xi^2.
\]
The requirements
\[
  N_1(-1)=1,
  \qquad
  N_1(0)=0,
  \qquad
  N_1(1)=0
\]
give
\[
  a=0,
  \qquad
  b=-\frac12,
  \qquad
  c=\frac12.
\]
Hence,
\[
  \boxed{
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi-1).
  }
\]
Applying the same nodal conditions to the other two nodes gives
\[
  \boxed{
  N_2(\xi)=1-\xi^2
  }
\]
and
\[
  \boxed{
  N_3(\xi)
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi+1).
  }
\]
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.1.1 Using Lagrange polynomials
The direct derivation above shows how a nodal shape function is determined from its interpolation conditions. The same functions can also be constructed systematically using Lagrange polynomials.
For a set of interpolation nodes with reference coordinates \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_n\), the Lagrange shape function \(N_i(\xi)\) is associated with node \(i\):
\[
  N_i(\xi)
  =
  \prod_{\substack{j=1\\j\ne i}}^n
  \frac{\xi-\xi_j}{\xi_i-\xi_j}.
\]
For example,
\[
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{\xi-\xi_2}{\xi_1-\xi_2}
  \frac{\xi-\xi_3}{\xi_1-\xi_3}
  =
  \frac{\xi}{-1}
  \frac{\xi-1}{-2}
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi-1).
\]
The remaining two functions follow in the same way.
The Lagrange construction is useful because it provides a systematic procedure for generating nodal interpolation functions once the interpolation nodes have been specified.
The three shape functions are collected in the shape-function matrix
\[
  \mathbf N(\xi)
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  N_1(\xi) & N_2(\xi) & N_3(\xi)
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The quadratic finite element displacement field is therefore written as
\[
  \boxed{
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf u_e.
  }
\]
The shape functions satisfy the partition-of-unity property,
\[
  N_1(\xi)+N_2(\xi)+N_3(\xi)=1.
\]
Consider a constant displacement field, for which
\[
  u_1=u_2=u_3=\bar u.
\]
The finite element interpolation then gives
\[
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf u_e
  =
  \left(
  N_1+N_2+N_3
  \right)\bar u
  =
  \bar u.
\]
Therefore, the partition-of-unity property ensures that a constant displacement field,
\[
  u\in\mathcal P_0,
\]
corresponding to a rigid translation of the bar, is reproduced exactly. Since such a field has zero strain, the element does not generate spurious deformation under rigid-body motion.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
section: 18.2 Regular isoparametric geometry and the strain–displacement matrix
text:
18.2 Regular isoparametric geometry and the strain–displacement matrix
The preceding chapter showed that a three-node isoparametric geometry does not necessarily produce a non-affine mapping. In particular, if the middle physical node lies exactly halfway between the two end nodes, the quadratic geometry interpolation reduces to an affine map.
We adopt that regular geometry here:
\[
  x_2=\frac{x_1+x_3}{2},
\]
with
\[
  L_e=x_3-x_1.
\]
Using
\[
  x(\xi)=\mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf x_e,
\]
the coordinate mapping becomes
\[
  x(\xi)
  =
  x_1+\frac{L_e}{2}(1+\xi),
\]
and therefore
\[
  \boxed{
  J=\frac{dx}{d\xi}=\frac{L_e}{2}.
  }
\]
The geometry is thus deliberately kept affine. The constant Jacobian allows us to isolate the effect of increasing the displacement interpolation order: in this regular case, \(\mathbf B(\xi)\) remains linear in \(\xi\). With a non-affine geometry, \(J\) would vary within the element and this simple polynomial structure would no longer hold.
Differentiating the quadratic shape functions gives
\[
  \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \xi-\frac12 &
  -2\xi &
  \xi+\frac12
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Using the derivative transformation established previously,
\[
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi},
\]
we obtain
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  =
  \frac{2}{L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \xi-\frac12 &
  -2\xi &
  \xi+\frac12
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
\]
Unlike the two-node bar, the strain–displacement matrix now varies within the element.
Consequently,
\[
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e
\]
is of degree at most one in \(\xi\). Since the coordinate mapping is affine, it is also of degree at most one in the physical coordinate \(x\). For constant \(E\) and \(A\), the same is true of stress and axial force.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.3 Element stiffness and numerical integration
The element stiffness matrix retains the same form used for the two-node bar,
\[
  \mathbf K_e
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf B(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  EA
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  J\,d\xi.
\]
What changes is the polynomial degree of the transformed integrand.
For the regular quadratic element with constant \(E\) and \(A\),
\[
  \mathbf B(\xi)\in\mathcal P_1,
\]
because the derivatives of the quadratic shape functions are linear and the Jacobian is constant. Therefore, each scalar entry of the stiffness integrand contains a product
\[
  B_i(\xi)B_j(\xi)\in\mathcal P_2.
\]
The complete transformed scalar stiffness integrands are thus quadratic in \(\xi\).
The Gauss–Legendre rule must therefore satisfy
\[
  2n_g-1\ge2,
\]
so the minimum exact rule has
\[
  \boxed{n_g=2.}
\]
This is the first direct numerical consequence of increasing the interpolation order. For the constant-property two-node bar, \(\mathbf B\) is constant and one Gauss point is sufficient; for the quadratic bar, \(\mathbf B\) varies linearly and two points are required.
For example,
\[
  K_{11}
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  B_1(\xi)^2EAJ\,d\xi,
\]
with
\[
  B_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{2}{L_e}
  \left(
  \xi-\frac12
  \right).
\]
The corresponding scalar integrand therefore contains the quadratic factor
\[
  \left(
  \xi-\frac12
  \right)^2.
\]
Evaluating the element integrals gives
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf K_e
  =
  \frac{EA}{3L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  7 & -8 & 1\\
  -8 & 16 & -8\\
  1 & -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
\]
Two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature reproduces this matrix exactly.
Using fewer quadrature points is not merely less accurate in this case. With one Gauss point, the quadratic element stiffness matrix develops an additional zero-energy mode. This consequence of under-integration is explored in the exercises.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.4 Consistent distributed loading
The consistent element load vector retains the same form,
\[
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf N(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  q\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  J\,d\xi.
\]
For a uniform distributed load,
\[
  q(x)=q_0,
\]
the only factor that varies with \(\xi\) is the quadratic shape function. Since
\[
  N_i(\xi)\in\mathcal P_2,
\]
while \(q_0\) and \(J\) are constant, each scalar load-vector integrand belongs to
\[
  \mathcal P_2.
\]
The minimum exact Gauss–Legendre rule therefore again has
\[
  \boxed{n_g=2.}
\]
This provides a second direct consequence of the higher-order interpolation. For the two-node bar with uniform loading, the corresponding load-vector integrands are linear and one Gauss point is sufficient. For the three-node quadratic bar, they are quadratic and require two points.
Evaluating the integrals gives
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \frac{q_0L_e}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
\]
The ratio
\[
  1:4:1
\]
is not an arbitrary distribution of the total load. Each nodal contribution is determined by the corresponding shape function through
\[
  f_{e,i}^q
  =
  q_0J
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  N_i(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Because the shape functions form a partition of unity, the nodal contributions also preserve the total distributed load
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^{3} f_{e,i}^q
  =
  q_0L_e.
\]
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
section: 18.5 What the quadratic approximation can reproduce
text:
18.5 What the quadratic approximation can reproduce
Having derived the quadratic element formulation, we can now ask a different question: which displacement fields can this richer approximation space represent exactly?
The approximation space of the three-node element contains all polynomial displacement fields up to degree two,
\[
  \mathcal P_0
  \subset
  \mathcal P_1
  \subset
  \mathcal P_2.
\]
If a displacement field belongs to one of these polynomial subspaces, the interpolation has the capability to represent it exactly. This property is commonly described as polynomial completeness or polynomial reproducibility.
The three cases have a direct mechanical interpretation:



Displacement field
Polynomial space
Mechanical interpretation




\(u=a\)
\(\mathcal P_0\)
rigid translation


\(u=a+bx\)
\(\mathcal P_1\)
constant strain


\(u=a+bx+cx^2\)
\(\mathcal P_2\)
linearly varying strain



Thus, increasing the interpolation order enlarges the set of displacement fields that the element can represent exactly. It does not require every finite element solution to contain a quadratic term.
The following two one-element problems make this distinction explicit. The first has an exact solution in the lower-order space \(\mathcal P_1\); the second uses the full quadratic space \(\mathcal P_2\).

18.5.1 End-force-only bar
Consider a bar of length \(L\), constant \(E\) and \(A\), fixed at
\[
  x=0
\]
and subjected to an axial force \(F\) at
\[
  x=L
\]
with no distributed load (\(q(x)=0\)).
The analytical solution is
\[
  u(x)
  =
  \frac{F}{EA}x.
\]
The displacement field is therefore linear.
Discretize the complete bar using one regular quadratic element,
\[
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=\frac L2,
  \qquad
  x_3=L.
\]
The nodal force vector is
\[
  \mathbf f_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  0\\
  0\\
  F
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Using the quadratic-element stiffness matrix and imposing
\[
  u_1=0,
\]
yields the reduced system
\[
  \frac{EA}{3L}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  16 & -8\\
  -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  0\\
  F
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its solution is
\[
  u_2
  =
  \frac{FL}{2EA},
  \qquad
  u_3
  =
  \frac{FL}{EA}.
\]
Substituting these values into the quadratic interpolation gives
\[
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \frac{FL}{EA}
  \left(
  \frac12N_2+N_3
  \right).
\]
Since
\[
  \frac12N_2+N_3
  =
  \frac{1+\xi}{2},
\]
and
\[
  x=\frac L2(1+\xi),
\]
we obtain
\[
  \boxed{
  u^h(x)=\frac{F}{EA}x.
  }
\]
For this problem, the quadratic element reproduces the linear solution exactly. The exact displacement field belongs to \(\mathcal P_1\), which is contained in the quadratic approximation space \(\mathcal P_2\).
The quadratic term is therefore not activated in this particular solution: the element represents the lower-order linear field exactly, and the corresponding strain is constant.


18.5.2 Uniformly loaded bar
Now consider the same bar subjected to a uniform distributed axial load \(q\), with
\[
  u(0)=0
\]
and no applied axial force at
\[
  x=L.
\]
For constant \(EA\),
\[
  -EA\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}=q,
\]
and the analytical solution is
\[
  \boxed{
  u(x)
  =
  \frac{q}{EA}
  \left(
  Lx-\frac{x^2}{2}
  \right),
  }
\]
which is a quadratic displacement field.
Using one regular quadratic element over the complete bar, the consistent load vector is
\[
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \frac{qL}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
After imposing
\[
  u_1=0,
\]
the reduced finite element equations become
\[
  \frac{EA}{3L}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  16 & -8\\
  -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \frac{qL}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The solution is
\[
  u_2
  =
  \frac{3qL^2}{8EA},
  \qquad
  u_3
  =
  \frac{qL^2}{2EA}.
\]
Substituting these nodal values into the interpolation gives
\[
  \boxed{
  u^h(x)
  =
  \frac{q}{EA}
  \left(
  Lx-\frac{x^2}{2}
  \right).
  }
\]
One quadratic element therefore reproduces the complete analytical displacement field exactly.
In this case,
\[
  u(x)\in\mathcal P_2,
\]
so the solution uses the full approximation space available to the element. Its derivative is linear, and the corresponding strain varies within the element.
Together, the two examples show that the polynomial order of the element describes its approximation capability, not the polynomial degree that every particular solution must exhibit.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.6 Response recovery
For the quadratic element,
\[
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e.
\]
Because \(\mathbf B\) varies linearly with \(\xi\), the finite element strain generally varies within the element. For constant \(E\) and \(A\), the same is true of
\[
  \sigma^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  E\varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
\]
and
\[
  N^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  A\sigma^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right).
\]
Response recovery therefore no longer produces, in general, a single strain, stress, or axial-force value for the complete element. These fields can be evaluated at any selected position within the element.
The locations used for response evaluation should not be confused with the quadrature points used to integrate the element equations. The same locations may be used for both purposes, but integration and response evaluation are different operations.
crumbs: One-dimensional continuum finite elements
18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

title: 18  The three-node quadratic axial-bar element
text:
18.7 Toward the MiniFEM implementation
The next implementation will reuse the existing isoparametric and Gauss–Legendre framework. Rather than constructing a new finite element workflow, we will adapt the verified two-node formulation to the quadratic interpolation developed in this chapter.
The main element-level changes are:

three local displacement DOFs instead of two;
quadratic shape functions and linear shape-function derivatives;
a strain–displacement matrix \(\mathbf B(\xi)\) that varies within the element;
two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature for the regular constant-property stiffness matrix and uniform distributed load;
response recovery for fields that can vary within the element.

The two one-element problems considered in this chapter provide reference cases for verifying the implementation. The end-force problem must reproduce the linear displacement field and constant strain exactly, whereas the uniformly loaded problem must reproduce the quadratic displacement field and linear strain exactly.
Once the quadratic element has been implemented and verified, we will move from exact polynomial reproduction to problems that require approximation, allowing us to introduce error measures and study convergence under mesh refinement.






TipExercises




Differentiate the partition-of-unity relation and verify that
\[ \frac{dN_1}{d\xi} + \frac{dN_2}{d\xi} + \frac{dN_3}{d\xi} =
0. \]
Explain why this is consistent with zero strain under a rigid translation.
Consider a linear displacement field \[
u(x)=a+bx.
\] Evaluate it at the three element nodes, \[
x_1,\qquad x_2=\frac{x_1+x_3}{2},\qquad x_3,
\] and show directly that the quadratic interpolation reproduces the original field exactly.
Evaluate the stiffness entry
\[
  K_{12}
\]
analytically and verify the corresponding entry of the closed-form element stiffness matrix.
Verify that
\[
  \mathbf K_e
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  1\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \mathbf 0.
\]
What physical displacement mode does this vector represent?
Evaluate the quadratic-element stiffness using one Gauss–Legendre point at
\[
  \xi=0.
\]
Construct the resulting stiffness matrix and identify the additional zero-energy mode.
Use partition of unity to show directly that the uniform consistent load vector preserves the total distributed load:
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^{3}f_{e,i}^q=q_0L_e.
\]
Suppose that \(q(x)\) varies linearly over the regular quadratic element.
Determine the polynomial degree of
\[
  N_i(\xi)q\!\left(x(\xi)\right)J
\]
and hence the minimum exact Gauss–Legendre rule.
Then derive the corresponding consistent nodal load vector.
For the end-force-only example, substitute the finite element nodal displacements into
\[
  \varepsilon^h(\xi)
  =
  \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e
\]
and show that the strain is constant.
Repeat the calculation for the uniformly loaded bar and show that the strain varies linearly.
The three-node bar developed in this chapter uses the local numbering
\[
  1 \;-\; 2 \;-\; 3,
\]
with node 2 at the element midpoint. In many finite element formulations, however, the two end nodes are numbered first and the midpoint node is numbered last. Relative to the numbering used in this chapter, the nodal positions are then reordered as
\[
  1 \;-\; 3 \;-\; 2.
\]
Thus, the alternative convention assigns local nodes 1 and 2 to the element ends and local node 3 to the midpoint. The finite element itself has not changed: only the ordering of the local nodal quantities has changed. This is useful to understand because element matrices depend on the chosen local DOF ordering, even though the underlying mechanical element and its physical predictions remain unchanged.
Starting from the quadratic element derived in this chapter, construct the element stiffness matrix for the local displacement vector
\[
  \mathbf u_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix},
\]
where nodes 1 and 2 are located at the two element ends and node 3 is the midpoint.
Show that the resulting stiffness matrix is
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf K_e
  =
  \frac{EA}{3L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  7 & 1 & -8\\
  1 & 7 & -8\\
  -8 & -8 & 16
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
\]
Verify this result in two different ways:

Reorder the rows and columns of the stiffness matrix derived in the chapter. You may do this using a permutation matrix. If
\[
  \mathbf u_e^{(123)}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
\]
denotes the ordering used in the chapter, with node 2 at the midpoint, and
\[
  \mathbf u_e^{(132)}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_3\\
  u_2
  \end{bmatrix}
\]
denotes the ordering with the two end nodes first, then
\[
  \mathbf u_e^{(132)}
  =
  \mathbf P\mathbf u_e^{(123)},
\]
with
\[
  \mathbf P
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & 0 & 0\\
  0 & 0 & 1\\
  0 & 1 & 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Use this transformation to show that
\[
  \boxed{
  \mathbf K_e^{(132)}
  =
  \mathbf P
  \mathbf K_e^{(123)}
  \mathbf P^{\mathsf T}.
  }
\]
Verify that this produces the matrix given above.
Verify the same result directly from the element formulation. For the new local ordering, first write the reordered shape-function matrix as \[
\mathbf N^{(132)}(\xi)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
N_1(\xi) & N_3(\xi) & N_2(\xi)
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Construct the corresponding \(\mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)\) and use \[
\mathbf K_e^{(132)}
=
\int_{-1}^{1}
\mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
EA
\mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)
J\,d\xi
\] to verify the stiffness matrix obtained by permutation.
Explain why the two stiffness matrices have different arrangements of their entries but represent exactly the same finite element.










ImportantKey points to remember




Increasing the interpolation order from linear to quadratic enlarges the approximation space from \(\mathcal P_1\) to \(\mathcal P_2\) without changing the underlying finite element procedure.
The quadratic Lagrange shape functions satisfy the nodal interpolation property \[
N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}
\] and form a partition of unity.
The approximation spaces are nested: \[
\mathcal P_0
\subset
\mathcal P_1
\subset
\mathcal P_2.
\] The quadratic element can therefore represent rigid translations, linear displacement fields with constant strain, and quadratic displacement fields with linearly varying strain.
The polynomial order of the element describes its approximation capability. It does not require every finite element solution to contain terms of the highest available order.
For the regular three-node element, \[
J=\frac{L_e}{2},
\] while \(\mathbf B(\xi)\) is linear in \(\xi\). For constant \(E\) and \(A\), strain, stress, and axial force can therefore vary linearly within the element.
For constant \(E\) and \(A\), the stiffness integrands and the uniform-load integrands are quadratic in \(\xi\). Two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature is the minimum exact rule for both.
The consistent nodal vector for a uniform distributed load is \[
\mathbf f_e^q
=
\frac{q_0L_e}{6}
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
4\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Increasing the interpolation order changes several connected parts of the element formulation: it enriches the approximation space, changes \(\mathbf B(\xi)\) and the variation of the recovered fields within the element, increases the polynomial degree of the element integrands, and can therefore increase the quadrature order required for exact integration.
